name: Rest Assured
subtitle: Because Death Should Rest in Peace — Not in Pieces.
description:
Obsidian, and a great deal of it. The stone does not reflect the violet overhead; it takes it in and returns nothing, so that the building reads at distance as a hole in the town cut roughly to the shape of a building. Fractal work is etched across the whole face of it, fine as frost, and it holds still under a direct look and is doing something else at the corner of the eye.

The slogan is over the door in letters of restrained gold: BECAUSE DEATH SHOULD REST IN PEACE — NOT IN PIECES. Inside, the silence is not the absence of noise. It is a maintained condition, the way a temperature is maintained, and it costs something to run.

The vaults go back further than the building goes back. Nobody who works here regards that as a fact about the building.
revisit: Soliloquy is where she was, at an angle she has not adjusted, and the count of vaults along the near wall is not the count you left with. You have stopped doing the count aloud. She noticed that you stopped, and approved, and said so in a way that took ninety seconds and rhymed twice.

lucid.2: The whispers in the air here are not consistent in language but are consistent in rhythm, and the rhythm is a sentence being composed rather than a sentence being spoken.
lucid.3: Under the whispering: paper. Not turning — being *fed*, drawn round a roller one line at a time, and then the small definite noise of a lever thrown at the end of it.
lucid.4: There is no whispering. There has never been whispering. There is a room somewhere with a machine in it, and this building is what the sound of that machine looks like when it is given somewhere to be.

ambient: The temperature in the west corridor drops eleven degrees between one vault and the next and comes back up again four vaults later, and the drop is not where the draught is, and there is no draught.
Your watch, which is stopped, is stopped at a different time in this room. You check it twice. It goes back to the old time on the stair down and neither reading has any business being a reading.

A whisper resolves for one whole second into a complete sentence — '...and furthermore, the arrangement was never—' — in a cadence you have heard every day of your life, and then goes back to being the sound of a cold building.
Soliloquy delivers eleven lines of something to the far end of an empty corridor, at volume, with feeling, and does not turn round afterwards to see whether anybody heard it.

The count of the vaults in the west corridor comes out at nineteen. You did not count them. You have simply arrived at the far end knowing the number, again, and it is a different number from the one you arrived with on Tuesday.

objects.name: the vault plates
objects.description:
Brass, recessed, one to a door, engraved to a standard that suggests an engraver paid by the hour who nonetheless enjoyed the work and took the extra minute on the serifs. Name, two dates, and a line of the family's choosing underneath.

The trick — and it is done to everyone who comes in here, and Soliloquy will confirm it without being asked and without being remotely helpful about it — is that on first look the plate carries your own name.

Not a resemblance and not a similar name. *Your* name, your spelling, with the middle one included, and the middle one is not a name you have said aloud since a form in 1994 and is not a name anybody in this parish has ever had occasion to learn.

It holds for less than a second. Then it is a stranger's name, and the stranger's dates are ordinary and unremarkable, and the family's chosen line is something about a garden.
objects.repeat: It happens on every plate and it has not stopped happening and it does not get less unpleasant with familiarity. Your name, your middle name, the one nobody in this parish has been told, engraved to a standard that took somebody a day per letter.

lucid.3: The second date on your name is not blank. You have never got a clean look at it and you have stopped pretending that is bad luck.

objects.monocle: The gold holds your name on the plate instead of letting it go. OLIVER OTTO ONIONS, and beneath it two dates, and the second one is legible and is not far off and is written in the same hand as the three dry pages in your notebook.

passive.text: Everyone gets this. That is the reported effect and Soliloquy confirms it. But everyone getting their own name is a mirror, and a mirror does not know a middle name that has not been spoken aloud in thirty years.

Watch Soliloquy while you read a plate. She does not watch the plate. She watches your face for the half-second the name is yours, and what is on her face is not amusement. It is the expression of somebody checking that a thing is still going wrong the way it is supposed to.

clue.title: Your name on every plate
clue.text: Every vault plate carries your full name — including a middle name unspoken in thirty years — for under a second before resolving to a stranger's.

clue.title: The second date
clue.text: Held under the monocle, your name stays on the plate, and the second date is legible, and it is written in the same hand as the three dry pages.

check.prompt: Nineteen vault plates, struck and mounted and engraved to a standard the trade abandoned two centuries ago. Read all of them, in order, and do not stop at the one with your name on it.
check.success:
Nineteen names. You know four of them and three of those four are people you have met tonight.

And the strike depth is not uniform: eighteen are stamped to the same depth, and one — the seventh — is shallower, and struck twice, the second strike slightly off the first, as though the name on it had been changed to itself.
check.failure:
Nineteen plates, brass, mounted, engraved to a standard nobody has met in two hundred years.

And one of them with your name on it, with the middle name, and after that the other eighteen are extremely difficult to give any attention to at all. You get to the fourth. You go back to the first. You get to the fourth again.

clue.title: Struck twice, to itself
clue.text: The seventh vault plate at Rest Assured is shallower than the rest and struck twice, the second strike slightly off — a name changed to itself.

objects.name: the unmarked vault
objects.description:
Third from the end of the west corridor, and it has no plate. Not a blank plate — no plate, no recess, no screw holes, no discolouration where a plate has been taken off. The door was made without provision for one.

The seam around it is not sealed. It stands very slightly ajar, at a width of perhaps two fingers, and it has stood at exactly that width every time you have been in this corridor. Through it there is light: warm, low, single-source, of the kind a lamp with a green shade makes.

You have never got closer than eight feet. Not because you are prevented. Because on each approach Soliloquy has arrived beside you with something to say, and the something has always been long, and by the end of it you have been somewhere else.
objects.repeat: Two fingers. Always two fingers. A door that has been standing open for eleven years in a building where the count of the doors will not hold still from one Tuesday to the next.

lucid.2: The light behind it moves when the whispering pauses.
lucid.4: It is not ajar. It is being *held* ajar, at a width somebody has chosen, so that the light gets out and you do not get in.

objects.monocle: Through the gold, the gap widens to the width of a doorway without the door moving, and behind it is your desk. Not a desk of the same make. Yours: the door on two trestles, the drift of paper, the trestle with the split in the left leg that you have been meaning to see to since before the water. And on it, in the rectangle where your dust says nothing has ever stood, a typewriter, with a page in it, and the page is not blank.

passive.text: Every single time. She arrives at eight feet, not seven, not nine. That is not vigilance. That is a marked position, and somebody marked it.

A door manufactured without provision for a plate was manufactured for a vault that was never going to be assigned an occupant. This one was not overlooked. It was built empty and kept empty and kept ajar.

check.prompt: She will arrive at your elbow at eight feet with something long and courteous to say. Get the question in first, and make it one she cannot answer in verse.
check.success:
You start talking before she does. You start on the slogan — on the em dash in it, on the decision to break REST IN PEACE against NOT IN PIECES on a hyphen that is doing the work of a whole theology, on whether a house that advertises against dismemberment is reassuring the bereaved or the merchandise.

It is not your best. It is your longest, and length is the currency here, and Soliloquy is a woman constitutionally unable to let a speech go unanswered. She answers. She answers at length, in rhyme, with a hand raised to hold her place — and a hand raised to hold a place is a hand not raised to stop you.

Seven feet. Six. At four you can see the split in the left trestle leg.

At three she stops mid-line, and the silence in this building is a maintained condition and she has just switched it off, and the sound underneath it is a machine typing very fast.

'Not that one,' she says, in her own voice, which you have not heard before and which has no rhyme in it at all. 'I have kept that one shut for you, Mr Onions, and I would like it noted that I have never once been thanked.'
check.failure:
You open on the slogan and she takes the em dash off you inside a sentence.

She has been waiting years for somebody to raise the em dash. What follows is nine minutes on punctuation as a mortuary practice, delivered without a breath you can get a foot into, and at some point during it you have been walked — gently, courteously, without a hand laid on you — back down the corridor to the vestibule, where the door is, and where the sound of a machine typing is not audible at all.

clue.title: Your desk, in a vault
clue.text: Behind the unmarked door: your desk. The split in the left trestle leg included. And on it, a typewriter, with a page in it that is not blank.

clue.title: Kept shut, deliberately
clue.text: Soliloquy does not guard the unmarked vault the way she guards the others. She guards it the way somebody guards a thing they have decided you should not have yet.

objects.name: the interment ledger
objects.description:
On a stand by the vestibule, open, because Soliloquy holds that the dead have nothing whatever to hide and that the living should be encouraged in the habit while there is still time for it to do them any good.

Columns: NAME. RECEIVED. VAULT. PAID BY. It runs back a very long way, in several hands, in one ink — which is its own small impossibility and not the one that matters tonight.

The PAID BY column is the one.

Family, family, estate, family, parish, family, family, estate. The ordinary distribution of who buries whom, in a parish where most people are buried by somebody who loved them and some are buried by the rates.

And then, at intervals with no pattern in them that you can find, a run of entries where that column reads only: ACCOUNT SETTLED IN ADVANCE BY THE COALITION.

Forty or so, scattered across six decades. The names in those rows are not remarkable. The dates are not remarkable. The vaults are ordinary vaults in ordinary corridors. Whatever those forty had in common, it is not written anywhere in this book.
objects.repeat: You count the Coalition rows again and get a different total, and the difference is not in the direction of more. There were forty on Tuesday. There are thirty-nine tonight, and the hand has not changed, and no page has been removed.
objects.monocle:
Through the gold the Coalition rows have a further column that the page does not otherwise carry.

It is headed REASON, and it is ruled in the same ink as the rest, and it has been there all along under the paper.

Every entry in it says the same three words. Forty rows, six decades, one hand: NOTICED TOO MUCH.

There is a forty-first row, ruled and waiting, with nothing in the name column yet.

passive.text: Settled in advance. Not settled — settled *in advance*. Somebody paid for these vaults before the people in them needed vaults, which means somebody knew, and the interesting question is not how they knew. It is how far in advance.
Soliloquy leaves this ledger open on a stand in the doorway. She wants it read. She has wanted it read for some time, by somebody who would do more than count.

clue.title: Settled in advance by the Coalition
clue.text: Forty-odd interments across several decades were paid for by the Quad-C before the occupants required them.

clue.title: NOTICED TOO MUCH
clue.text: Under the monocle the prepaid rows carry a column the page does not have. Every entry reads: NOTICED TOO MUCH.

check.prompt: The ledger is open on a stand in a public vestibule and the hand is copperplate throughout. Go at it as a document — the columns, the totals, the conventions of the trade — rather than as a list of the dead.
check.success:
Vault ledgers run to a form, and the form has been the same for two hundred years: date of lease, name of lessee, term, and a countersign.

This one has all four columns and the dates in the first column are *later* than the countersigns in the fourth. Every entry was signed off before it was made. For nineteen vaults. In copperplate, without a single correction, which is not how a man writes when he is making it up as he goes.
check.failure: Copperplate, four columns, two hundred years of convention behind it. Something about the ordering is wrong and the wrongness will not resolve into a sentence, and the keeper is watching you not resolve it with enormous courtesy.

clue.title: Countersigned before it was written
clue.text: Every entry in the Rest Assured ledger was countersigned before its own lease date. Nineteen vaults, no corrections.

objects.name: a brass plaque with no name on it
objects.description:
Set into the wall of the vestibule at the height of a plate, in the same brass as the vault plates, cut by what is unmistakably the same hand — the same slightly open O, the same way of finishing a stroke.

It carries no name. It carries no dates. It carries a number, five digits, engraved.

Engraved. That is the whole of the problem and it does not get smaller with looking. Not printed, not painted, not displayed on any mechanism — there is no mechanism, the brass is solid, you have put a hand flat on the wall either side of it and there is nothing behind it but stone. The digits are *cut into brass*, permanently, by a tool, in the way that a thing is cut when it is intended never to change.

It was 04412 the first time you saw it. It was 04409 on Tuesday.

It is not 04409 now.
objects.repeat: Lower. Always lower. Nobody has been near it, there is no mechanism behind the plate, the chisel marks are old — and the number is lower than it was when you came up the hill this evening.
objects.monocle: The gold shows the brass mid-cut: a burin in the metal, moving, unheld, and behind it the ghosts of every number it has been, stacked back through 04412 and past it, thousands of them, all the way to a first cut that is out of sight below the plaque and going down.

passive.text: A counter has a mechanism. This has a chisel mark. Somebody is re-engraving a brass plaque, by hand, at a rate you have not caught, to keep a count that nobody has posted the purpose of.

Five digits, on a plate, in a mausoleum, unlabelled. The absence of the label is the message: everybody who needs to know what it counts down to already knows, and the plaque is not there to inform them. It is there so they cannot say they were not warned.

clue.title: The engraved countdown
clue.text: A nameless brass plaque in the vestibule carries five hand-engraved digits. The number falls. No mechanism is involved and no purpose is posted.

check.prompt: The countdown is running and it is running toward something. Stand here and watch it without looking away and without deciding in advance what it means.
check.success:
You hold. It runs. It does not speed up because you are watching and it does not stop because you would prefer it to, and after a while the important thing about it becomes clear, which is that it is not a threat.

It is a *deadline*. Somebody set it. Somebody has been working against it. And a deadline is the only kind of clock that can be missed on purpose.
check.failure:
You hold for as long as you hold, and then the arithmetic gets into you — how long, and until what, and what happens to a parish when a clock somebody else set runs out — and you are looking at the wall instead, and the wall is a great deal easier.

When you look back the count is lower and you have no idea by how much.

clue.title: A deadline, not a threat
clue.text: The countdown at Rest Assured is a deadline somebody set and has been working against — the only kind of clock that can be missed on purpose.

objects.name: the whispers
objects.description:
They travel through the air rather than along the stone, which is the wrong way round for a building of this shape and this material, and anybody who has spent a night in a stone building knows it is the wrong way round.

They are constant. They do not rise or fall with the draught, they do not stop when the outer door closes, and they are almost words — near enough that the ear keeps going back to them the way a tongue goes back to a chipped tooth.

Stand still and give them a minute and they resolve. Not into a voice, which is what you would expect and could dismiss. Into a *sentence*: assembled out of the general susurrus by the same trick that assembles a face out of wallpaper, except that the face out of wallpaper does not have grammar in it and this does.

They are all on one subject. They are about death, and they are about dreams, and they never once mention either without mentioning the other in the same clause — and the construction of them is careful, and balanced, and worked-over, in a way that overheard speech has never been in the history of anybody overhearing anything.
objects.repeat: They have got easier to resolve, which is not the direction these things are supposed to travel in. On Tuesday it was weather. Tonight there are words in it, and the words are in your cadence.
objects.monocle: The gold does nothing to them, because they are not visual, and the failure is informative: the monocle reveals what a thing is made of, and it has no opinion about these at all, the way it has no opinion about your own voice.

check.prompt: Stop trying to hear the words. The words are not the information. Listen for *who is talking*, and how many of them there are, and whose cadence they are using.
check.success:
You stop reaching for the words and let the room have them, and what comes up out of the susurrus is not vocabulary. It is cadence.

It is yours. Every whisper in this building is in your cadence — the long clause, the qualifying aside, the pause before the last word that you have never once managed to stop putting there. Forty voices, none of them yours, all of them speaking the way you speak.

They are not the dead. They are not talking about you. They are *drafts* of you, and this is where they have been put.
check.failure: You listen for the speaker and get the words instead, and the words this time are '—should rest in peace, not in—' and then the building's slogan, and then the slogan again, and then a stretch that is only the rhythm of the slogan with different syllables in it, and none of it will hold still long enough to have said anything.

clue.title: Forty voices, one cadence
clue.text: The whispers in Rest Assured are all in your cadence. Not the dead, and not about you: drafts of you, stored.

objects.name: the unmarked vault, standing open
objects.description:
Two fingers has become a doorway.

The measurement Soliloquy has taken every Michaelmas for eleven years with the same two fingers of the same hand — the only measurement in the whole of Silvora Reefs that has never once disagreed with itself, the fixed point she has been navigating by since before you moved into a building that hangs from nothing — has finally disagreed with itself.

The door stands open on a room that is warm and lit and nine feet by eleven. There is no draught through it now. The air on both sides is the same air.

She is standing beside it with her hands folded and she is not saying anything at all — no verse, no couplet, no address to the horizontal — in a building where silence is a maintained condition and she is the one who has been maintaining it for sixty years.

She does not tell you not to go. She has decided not to, at some cost, and the cost is visible, and she would prefer you did not comment on it.
objects.monocle: The gold shows the desk, the split trestle, the green lamp, the page in the machine — and a second chair, which has not been there before, drawn up at an angle that means somebody expects to be talked to.
objects.repeat: Still open. It is not going to close on its own, and that is not the same thing as it being patient, and Soliloquy has stopped arriving at your elbow when you stand in front of it.

passive.text: Every deduction you have made for a fortnight terminates here. There is nothing further to work out. The next thing is not a conclusion, it is a step.
Four inches of nothing, and a floor on the other side that will take a man's weight. The body has already decided. It has been leaning that way since the harbour.

check.prompt:
Go through. Nothing is stopping you and nothing has been stopping you for some time, and that is the part that will need thinking about afterwards, on the other side, if there is an afterwards and if there is a side.

There is no way back through a seam. Whatever is unfinished in Silvora Reefs stays unfinished.
check.success:
You go through.

There is no membrane and no cold and no drama, and the last thing behind you is somebody not saying anything, and then you are standing on boards in a room nine feet by eleven with a green-shaded lamp in it.
check.failure:
Your foot goes over the edge and your weight does not follow it, and you stand for a while in a doorway with one leg committed, which is not a dignified way to arrive anywhere and is a completely honest description of the last fortnight.

Then the knee that has been going since the harbour makes the decision for you, and you go through badly, and land on boards, in a room nine feet by eleven, with a green-shaded lamp in it.

objects.name: the vault that stands open
objects.description:
West corridor, past the count that will not settle: one obsidian door standing about two fingers off its jamb, and it has stood that way for as long as anybody in this building has been asked about it.

The stone is very black and very cold and takes a fingerprint beautifully, and it is entirely free of fingerprints, which in a building this old is its own kind of statement.

Soliloquy's position — delivered in couplets, at length, and with the specific fluency of a woman who has answered this question before — is that it is not open, it is *unclosed*, and that the distinction is the whole of her profession and the reason there is a keeper here at all. She will not be drawn further. She will also not let you put a hand on it, and she does not make a performance of preventing you; she simply arrives at your elbow, courteously, every single time, and stays there until you have moved on.
objects.repeat: Two fingers. You have measured it with the same two fingers on four separate visits and it has been the same on all four, in a building where nothing else has agreed with itself twice.
objects.monocle: Through the gold the gap has a hand in it, holding the door off the jamb, and the hand is not straining. It has been resting there a long time and could close it whenever it liked.

passive.text: The draught goes the wrong way. Air moves *into* a two-finger gap in a sealed obsidian vault, continuously, and has to be going somewhere.

clue.title: Not open. Unclosed.
clue.text: A vault in the west corridor stands two fingers off its jamb and has for years. Soliloquy insists it is unclosed rather than open, and will not let anyone touch it.

check.prompt: A door does not come to rest two fingers open and stay there for eleven years. Stop looking at the gap and read the jamb.
check.success:
Obsidian is unforgiving and keeps everything, which makes this easy once you stop looking at the gap and start looking at the jamb.

There is scoring. Two arcs, one above the other, at the height a hand would take a door — and they are not the scoring of something forced. They are wear, of the kind that comes from a thing being drawn to exactly this position and released, over and over, a very large number of times.

This door is not stuck. It is *set*. Somebody opens it and closes it on a rhythm and two fingers is where it rests in between, and the last time it moved, going by the dust in the lower arc, was four days ago.
check.failure: Black stone, black shadow, and a lamp Soliloquy declines to move for you. The jamb gives up its width and nothing else, and she stands at the end of the corridor throughout, in couplets, being helpful in the way that prevents help.

clue.title: The gap is maintained
clue.text: Wear arcs on the vault jamb show the door has been drawn to exactly this position and released a great many times. It is not stuck open — it is kept open, on a rhythm, and it last moved four days ago.

objects.name: the parish, from up here
objects.description:
The mausoleum stands above everything, which is the point of a mausoleum, and from the west corridor's one window the whole of Silvora Reefs is laid out beneath the fog in the green of its own lamps.

You can see the harbour road and the roof of Durry Kwain. You can see the queue outside Mary's, moving, always moving. You can see the smoke off Ben's, going up through a roof that has no vent in it, and the lit sign at the Möbius holding its coil, and one window burning on the second floor of a building that hangs from nothing.

From this height it is possible to watch an entire town do its evening at once — every lit room, every errand, every small ordinary act of maintenance, simultaneously, in one glance.

Nobody who lives down there has any reason to come up here and look at it.

Soliloquy does it nightly. She has never mentioned this to anybody, and there is a chair by the window, and the chair faces out.
objects.repeat: The lamps are still on. The town is still doing its evening, all of it at once, in one view. Somebody down there has just closed a shutter, and somebody else has just opened a door onto a lit hallway and gone in.
objects.monocle: Through the gold the town is a page seen from the top corner, and the lamps are not lamps, they are the places where the writing is densest, and there are large areas with nothing on them at all.

clue.title: The whole parish, visible at once
clue.text: The west corridor window at Rest Assured overlooks all of Silvora Reefs. Soliloquy watches the town do its evening from here nightly and has never mentioned it.

check.prompt: The whole town is down there at once, doing the same eleven minutes of its evening. Take all of it in together rather than one lamp at a time.
check.success:
Every light in Silvora Reefs, and behind every light a person, and behind every person a small maintenance being performed on a town that nobody has told them is failing.

Luigi doing the west end first. Bud saying it is a light well to a ceiling that has not asked. Woolbinkle putting one on at nine because he had a feeling. Wino-T setting down a cup for a man in a mirror. Landy writing RESOLVED in a book. Darek wiping a counter that does not need it, at the window, watching the water.

None of them knows the others are doing it. Every single one of them is holding up their own eight feet of a building that has no business standing — and the town is not being kept up by whoever wrote it. It is being kept up by two hundred people independently refusing to let go of their own corner of it.
check.failure: Lamps in fog, and a town going about its evening, and it is beautiful from here and it does not add up to anything but a town. The parish keeps its own counsel and the window is cold and after a while there is nothing to do but come away from it.

clue.title: Two hundred people, each holding their own corner
clue.text: Seen whole from the mausoleum window: every Reefer is independently performing a small maintenance on a failing town — the route, the denial, the cans, the cup, the counter. None knows the others are doing it. The parish is not held up by its author.

exits.hang_hi: down out of the obsidian to a floor that hangs from nothing
exits.durry_kwain: down the hill toward vanilla, which after this will be welcome
exits.mobius: along and down to the red frontage and the light that is nearly red
exits.giddyup: along the ridge to smoke, and a table with names under it
